1.content: Create and run a native QuickGUI app with Solid. QuickGUI lets you build native desktop applications with Solid. There is no DOM or webview: Solid updates a retained tree that QuickGUI lays out and renders on the GPU.
1.keywords: install create cli window bun macos

2.content: macOS 13 or newer Bun 1.3 or newer Xcode Command Line Tools The Solid host currently targets macOS. The Rust framework also compiles for Windows and Linux, but those platforms are not yet the supported path for Solid applications.

3.content: Scaffold a project and start its native development app: The development command watches your source and replaces the running app only after the next build opens its first native window.

4.content: Application and window APIs come from @quickgui/native . Solid components and the renderer come from @quickgui/solid . Always await app.whenReady() before creating the first window. Each Window owns its renderer root and disposes it when the window closes.

5.content: On macOS, a production build is written under dist/darwin-* . Signing and notarization can be configured when you are ready to distribute.

6.content: Learn how Solid rendering and state work. Compose the unstyled components . Add real SwiftUI controls on macOS.

7.content: Understand the files in a generated Solid project. A generated project stays intentionally small. Your TSX runs in a Bun worker while QuickGUI keeps the platform event loop on the native main thread.

8.content: Put application UI in src/ . Add files and directories to production bundles through the resources option.

9.content: The entry module waits for the native app, creates windows, and passes a Solid root to createRenderer . Source modules may use ordinary Bun APIs. Keep native application and window work asynchronous at the hosted boundary.

10.content: quickgui.config.ts tells the CLI what to compile and package. Release-only options cover icons, signing, notarization, the Mac App Store, and updater manifests.

12.content: Use Solid reactivity to render retained native UI. QuickGUI uses Solid for composition and reactivity while the Rust core owns retained native state, layout, rendering, input, and accessibility.

13.content: createRenderer mounts one Solid root into a Window . JSX creates retained QuickGUI nodes rather than DOM elements. Signals update only the affected retained properties. QuickGUI redraws damaged regions and stays idle when nothing changes.

14.content: Use ordinary Solid signals, memos, resources, and control flow. Native callbacks enter Solid asynchronously. A callback receives the result already decided by the core; JavaScript never synchronously asks the native main thread for a value.

15.content: Create windows after app.whenReady() . Re-create the main window from the reopen event when macOS activates an app with no visible windows.

16.content: Use useWindow() from a component mounted by a QuickGUI window renderer when an action belongs to that window.

17.content: The Solid router projects QuickGUI's core-owned route table and bounded memory history. Use Link , Outlet , useLocation , useParams , useSearchParams , useNavigate , and useRouter below Router .

18.content: Lay out and style native nodes with familiar properties. QuickGUI styles retained native nodes with a typed style object. The names are familiar, but values are resolved by QuickGUI rather than a browser.

20.content: Flexbox is the default layout tool for rows, columns, alignment, gaps, wrapping, and flexible sizing.

23.content: Declare hover, active, focus, disabled, and selected paint directly on the node. The core applies the state without a JavaScript round trip.

24.content: Choose between primitives and accessible compound components. QuickGUI ships low-level primitives and accessible compound component families. They are unstyled: the core supplies behavior and semantics while your app supplies every visible surface.
24.keywords: view text button tabs checkbox unstyled

25.content: Use View , Text , Button , Input , TextArea , Markdown , Image , Svg , Shader , VirtualList , and Terminal as the retained building blocks.

26.content: A compound family exposes named parts. The root coordinates state and the Rust core owns keyboard behavior, focus, accessibility relationships, mount policy, and exact interaction deadlines.

27.content: Most roots accept a controlled value and matching callback, plus a default* value for uncontrolled use. The callback reports the result accepted by the core. Update the signal to keep a controlled declaration in sync.

35.content: Low-level inputs report a QuickGuiEvent ; compound value callbacks receive the normalized value first and the event second. Native decisions are delivered asynchronously after the core handles the interaction.

36.content: Present in-window overlays and operating-system dialogs. QuickGUI has in-window overlays, native child-window popovers, and operating-system dialogs. Choose the surface based on what may escape the current window and who owns its behavior.
36.keywords: popover dialog overlay alert file picker

37.content: Popover stays in the current retained window. Compose its trigger, portal, positioner, popup, and optional arrow or backdrop. The core flips and re-aligns a preferred placement when it would collide with the viewport.

38.content: Dialog contains focus, restores previous focus on dismissal, and holds closing content mounted for an exact exitDuration . Use AlertDialog for consequential confirmation. It refuses backdrop dismissal by default.

39.content: SystemPopover creates a native child window, so its content can extend beyond the owner window.

40.content: File pickers, message boxes, and similar operating-system dialogs come from @quickgui/native . Their results are Promise-based.

41.content: Mount real SwiftUI controls inside a Solid application. The SwiftUI bridge mounts real native SwiftUI controls inside a Solid-rendered QuickGUI window on macOS.
41.keywords: swiftui host slider toggle picker native

42.content: Host is one retained QuickGUI layout leaf backed by NSHostingView . Put SwiftUI bridge components below it.

43.content: The bridge exports Button , Slider , Toggle , ProgressView , Stepper , TextField , SecureField , Picker , SegmentedControl , DatePicker , ColorPicker , and Gauge . Each one has a dedicated reference page in the sidebar.

44.content: Values remain controlled by Solid. Native changes arrive through the matching callback.

45.content: By default, QuickGUI lays out Host like any other retained node. Set matchContents to use SwiftUI's intrinsic size on both axes, or choose { horizontal: true } or { vertical: true } .

46.content: SwiftUI hosting is the macOS bridge. Use ordinary @quickgui/solid components for cross-platform UI.

47.content: Style SwiftUI controls and host QuickGUI content back inside them. SwiftUI modifiers let Solid declare native appearance while reverse hosting lets SwiftUI content contain an ordinary QuickGUI subtree.
47.keywords: modifier glass quickguihostview popover reverse host

48.content: Import modifier factories from @quickgui/solid/swift-ui/modifiers and apply them in order. Available factories include buttonStyle , buttonBorderShape , controlSize , labelStyle , tint , and disabled .

49.content: On systems that provide it, the SwiftUI button bridge can request the native glass button style. The operating system remains responsible for the final rendering.

50.content: QuickGUIHostView mounts one ordinary QuickGUI subtree back inside a SwiftUI hierarchy.

51.content: The SwiftUI Popover composes a native SwiftUI trigger. Its content can use QuickGUIHostView when the popover body is built with ordinary QuickGUI components.
